title: Connecting reading to experience
keyIdea: Good readers link a story to their own life: this reminds me of when I… The best link is when the same thing happened to you or you felt the same way, not just the same name or the same word. Your own feelings help you guess how a character feels, but the words in the story come first: a character can feel differently from you. What you know about the world helps you guess what happens next, and a time you felt something helps you work out a new word.
familyTip: When you read a bedtime story, stop at a big moment and ask: has that ever happened to you? How did you feel? Then ask: does the girl in the story feel the same? Point to the words that show it. If your child says 'I have a dog too', ask what happened in the story and whether that has happened to them.

visual.caption: Does each memory really link to a story about a lost teddy? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: only a word is the same
items: I lost my blanket and cried.
My toy rabbit was lost at the park.
I could not find my best toy at bedtime.
I saw a bear at the zoo.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: link each story to the right memory, borrow a feeling, tap the clue word, guess what happens next and work out new words.

kid: When you read, stop and think. Has this ever happened to me? Say it out loud. This reminds me of when I lost my teddy.
A good link is the same thing, or the same feeling. My cat is called Tom does not help with a story about Tom getting lost. I got lost in a shop once does.
Think how you felt. Then you can guess how the boy in the book feels. But read the words too. You might be scared of the dentist. If Leo smiles, Leo is happy.
What you know helps. You know snow melts in the sun. So you can guess what happens to the snowman. A new word? Think of a time you felt it.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. The national curriculum for England asks Year 1 pupils to link what they read or hear to their own experiences, and Year 2 pupils to draw on what they already know or on background information and vocabulary. Reading researchers call these text-to-self and text-to-world connections. They work because a reader fills the gaps a story leaves with what they already know.

Not every link helps. A useful link matches what happens or how someone feels (I lost my mum in a shop too). A weak link only shares a surface detail: the same name, the same object or a favourite colour. Ask your child what happened in the story and whether that has happened to them, so the link carries meaning rather than a word.

Common mistakes: making surface links that do not explain anything; assuming a character feels what the child would feel and ignoring the words that say otherwise (he smiles, she hides her face); drifting into a long story of their own and losing the book; and guessing what happens next from a wish rather than from what they know about the world. Model the habit: this reminds me of... so I think she feels... let me check the words.

In the lab your child drags the memory that fits five story lines, borrows a feeling from their own life for five events, taps the clue word in four stories where the character feels differently from most people, picks what happens next using everyday knowledge, and works out four new words (soaked, exhausted, delicious, shivered) from a time they felt them.

practice.prompt: A story says: Ollie’s ice cream falls on the ground. Which memory helps you understand Ollie?
choices: My ice cream fell once and I was sad.
practice.hint: Look for a time the same thing happened to you.
practice.explain: Your ice cream fell too, so you know Ollie feels sad. Having a friend called Ollie, or liking green, tells you nothing about the story.

practice.prompt: Ben reads {n} stories. {k} of them remind him of something that happened to him. How many do not?
practice.hint: Take the stories that remind him away from all the stories.
practice.explain: {n} stories take away {k} that remind him leaves {=n-k}. Ben can still enjoy those, and learn about lives not like his.

practice.prompt: You love loud music. In the story, Ana covers her ears at the loud party. How does Ana feel?
choices: She does not like the noise.
practice.hint: Read what Ana does. What does covering your ears show?
practice.explain: Covering her ears shows Ana does not like the noise. You love loud music, but the story’s words show how Ana feels.

practice.prompt: In a story, Zak waits {a} days for his birthday. Then he waits {b} more days for his party. How many days does he wait in all?
practice.hint: Add the days for his birthday and the days for his party.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} days. You may know how long waiting feels, so you can guess Zak gets more and more excited.

practice.prompt: Raj has no coat, and it starts to rain. What happens next?
practice.hint: What happens to you when you are out in the rain with no coat?
practice.explain: You know rain makes you wet, so Raj gets wet. Getting hot or turning into a fish does not fit what you know.

pool.prompt: Which is a good link to a story about a girl who is shy at a party?
choices: I felt shy at a party and stood by Mum.
pool.hint: A good link is the same feeling or the same thing happening.
pool.explain: Feeling shy at a party is the same feeling as the girl. A party hat and a birthday month only share a word.

pool.prompt: Tom’s sandcastle is washed away by a wave. How does Tom feel?
pool.hint: Think of a time something you made got broken.
pool.explain: When something you made is spoiled, you feel sad. Tom feels sad too.

pool.prompt: You are scared of big dogs. In the story, Mia runs to hug the big dog and laughs. How does Mia feel?
pool.hint: Read what Mia does: she runs to hug it and laughs.
pool.explain: Running to hug the dog and laughing show Mia is happy. You might feel scared, but the story’s words show Mia feels happy.

pool.prompt: The puppy was famished, so it gobbled up its dinner. Think of how you eat when you are very hungry. What does famished mean?
pool.hint: The puppy gobbled up its dinner. When do you eat like that?
pool.explain: You gobble your food when you are very hungry, so famished means very hungry.

pool.prompt: Dan leaves his chocolate in the hot car. What happens next?
pool.hint: What does heat do to chocolate?
pool.explain: You know heat melts chocolate, so it melts. It does not turn into a cake, and a hot car does not make it cold.

pool.prompt: A book has {n} pages. On {k} pages you thought, this reminds me of when I… On how many pages did you not make a link?
pool.hint: Take the pages with a link away from all the pages.
pool.explain: {n} pages take away {k} pages with a link leaves {=n-k}. You do not need a link on every page.

pool.prompt: Which sentence shows a reader linking a story to their life?
choices: This reminds me of when my tooth fell out.
The book has a red cover.
pool.hint: Which one starts with this reminds me of when I…?
pool.explain: This reminds me of when my tooth fell out links what happens in the story to the reader’s own life. The cover and reading fast are not about what happens.

pool.prompt: Lily goes to a new school. On day 1 she has {a} friends. Each day after, she makes 1 more. How many friends does she have on day {d}?
pool.hint: On day 1 she has {a}. Add 1 for every day after day 1.
pool.explain: Day 1 is {a}, and there are {=d-1} days after it, so {a} + {=d-1} = {=a+d-1}. Maybe you also felt shy at first, then made friends.
